results.title: Bi-invariant linear orders on a group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a group $G$, the bi-invariant orders of $G$ are the linear orders $\le$ on $G$ (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive and total relations) that are invariant under left and right multiplication: for all $a, b, c \in G$, $a \le b$ implies $ca \le cb$ and $ac \le bc$.

results.summary: The statement that there is a finitely presented group $G$ that admits a bi-invariant linear order and has a finite generating family $g_1, \dots, g_k$ for which the word problem is insoluble: no algorithm decides, given a word in the $g_i$ and their inverses, whether it equals $1$ in $G$.

results.title: Doob's L² maximal inequality, finite horizon
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure and let $(f_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_k)$ and $\mu$ such that every $f_k$ is in $L^2(\mu)$. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\int (\max_{k \le n} |f_k|)^2 \, d\mu \le 4 \int f_n^2 \, d\mu$.

results.title: Predictable quadratic variation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\Omega$, let $(\mathcal{F}_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a filtration and let $(f_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued process. The predictable quadratic variation of $f$ with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_k)$ and $\mu$ is the process defined pointwise by $A_n(\omega) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbb{E}_\mu(f_{k+1} - f_k)^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_k$, so $A_0 = 0$. For a square-integrable martingale this is…

results.title: Expectation of the predictable quadratic variation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure and let $(f_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a real-valued martingale with respect to a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_k)$ and $\mu$ such that every $f_k$ is in $L^2(\mu)$, and let $A_n$ be its predictable quadratic variation. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\int A_n \, d\mu = \int f_n^2 \, d\mu - \int f_0^2 \, d\mu$.

results.title: Valid orderings of finite sets of nonzero integers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every finite set $A$ of nonzero integers has a valid ordering: its elements can be listed as $a_1, \dots, a_m$, each exactly once, so that the partial sums $a_1, a_1 + a_2, \dots, a_1 + \cdots + a_m$ are pairwise distinct. The empty sum $0$ is not counted among the partial sums.

results.title: Zero-sum subsequences of cross number at most one (Geroldinger; Elledge–Hurlbert)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a finite abelian group of order $|\Gamma|$. Every sequence $g_1, \dots, g_{|\Gamma|}$ of $|\Gamma|$ elements of $\Gamma$ has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence with cross number at most one: there is a nonempty set $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, |\Gamma|\}$ of indices with $\sum_{i \in S} g_i = 0$ and $\sum_{i \in S} 1/\operatorname{ord}(g_i) \le 1$, where $\operatorname{ord}(g_i)$ is the order of $g_i$.

results.title: Lemke–Kleitman theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every positive integer $n$, every sequence $g_1, \dots, g_n$ of $n$ elements of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence with cross number at most one: there is a nonempty set $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ of indices with $\sum_{i \in S} g_i = 0$ and $\sum_{i \in S} 1/\operatorname{ord}(g_i) \le 1$, where $\operatorname{ord}(g_i)$ is the additive order of $g_i$. The theorem is due to Lemke…

results.title: Good sequences in a finite abelian group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a finite abelian group, written additively, and let $g = (g_1, \dots, g_t)$ be a sequence of $t$ elements of $\Gamma$. The sequence $g$ is *good* if there is a nonempty set $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, t\}$ of indices with $\sum_{i \in S} g_i = 0$ whose cross number $\sum_{i \in S} 1/|g_i|$ is at most $1$, where $|g_i|$ is the order of $g_i$.

results.title: Probability that a random sequence is good
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a finite abelian group and $t \ge 0$ an integer. A sequence $g_1, \dots, g_t$ in $\Gamma$ is good if some nonempty set $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, t\}$ of indices has $\sum_{i \in S} g_i = 0$ and $\sum_{i \in S} 1/\operatorname{ord}(g_i) \le 1$, where $\operatorname{ord}(g_i)$ is the order of $g_i$. The good-sequence probability of $\Gamma$ at length $t$ is the number of good sequences of length $t$ in…

results.title: Good-sequence probability at length zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite abelian group $\Gamma$, the probability that a uniformly random sequence of length $0$ in $\Gamma$ is good equals $0$: the empty sequence has no nonempty zero-sum subsequence, so it is not good.

results.title: Half-good threshold
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite abelian group $\Gamma$, $P_{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is the least $t \ge 0$ such that a uniformly random sequence of $t$ elements of $\Gamma$ is good (has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence with cross number at most one) with probability at least $1/2$, that is, such that at least half of the $|\Gamma|^t$ sequences of length $t$ are good. If no such $t$ exists, $P_{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is defined to be $0$.

results.title: Half-good threshold of a group of order at most two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $\Gamma$ is a finite abelian group with at most two elements, then its half-good threshold $P_{1/2}(\Gamma)$ equals $1$.

A function $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a *threshold function* for $P$ if $t(k) > 0$ for all sufficiently large $k$ and, for every function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $P(k, f(k)) \to 1$ as $k \to \infty$ whenever $t = o(f)$, and…

results.title: Positive multiples of threshold functions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$. If $t$ is a threshold function for $P$ and $c > 0$ is a real number, then $k \mapsto c \, t(k)$ is also a threshold function for $P$.

results.title: Lagarias–Saks pebbling step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$, and let $w$ assign a natural-number cost $w(uv)$ to each unordered pair of vertices $\{u, v\}$. For configurations $C, C' : V \to \mathbb{N}$, there is a pebbling step from $C$ to $C'$ if there is an edge $uv$ of $G$ with $0 < w(uv) \le C(u)$ such that $C'$ is obtained from $C$ by removing $w(uv)$ pebbles from $u$ and adding one pebble to $v$.

results.title: Solvable pebbling configurations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a vertex set $V$ with natural-number edge costs $w$. A configuration $C : V \to \mathbb{N}$ of pebbles is *solvable* if for every target vertex $r$ there is a finite, possibly empty, sequence of pebbling steps on $G$ with costs $w$ leading from $C$ to a configuration with at least one pebble on $r$.

results.title: Configurations covering every vertex are solvable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph with natural-number edge costs $w$. Every pebbling configuration $C$ on $G$ with $C(r) \ge 1$ for every vertex $r$ is solvable with respect to $G$ and $w$.

results.title: Probability that a random pebbling configuration is solvable

results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ with $n$ vertices, let $w$ assign a natural-number cost to each unordered pair of vertices, and let $t \ge 0$ be an integer. A configuration of $t$ pebbles is a function $C : V \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{v \in V} C(v) = t$. The value is the number of configurations of $t$ pebbles that are solvable with respect to $G$ and $w$, divided by the number of all…

results.title: The solvability probability is at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set with natural-number edge costs $w$ and every $t \ge 0$, the probability that a uniformly random configuration of $t$ pebbles on $G$ is solvable is at most $1$.

results.title: Grid graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $d$ and $k$, the $d$-dimensional grid $P_k^d = \square_{i\lt d} P_k$ is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, k-1\}^d$ in which $x$ and $y$ are adjacent when there is a coordinate $i$ with $x_j = y_j$ for all $j \ne i$ and $|x_i - y_i| = 1$. For $k = 2$ this is the $d$-cube $Q_d$.

results.title: Grid edge costs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $d$ and $k$ be natural numbers and let $w_0, \dots, w_{d-1}$ be natural numbers. The grid cost with cost $w_i$ in coordinate $i$ assigns to each unordered pair $\{x, y\}$ of points of $\{0, \dots, k-1\}^d$ the sum of the $w_i$ over the coordinates $i$ with $x_i \ne y_i$. On an edge of the grid exactly one coordinate differs, so an edge in coordinate $i$ costs $w_i$.

results.title: Grid cost of a pair differing in one coordinate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ and $k$ be natural numbers, let $w_0, \dots, w_{d-1}$ be natural numbers, let $x, y \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}^d$, and let $i \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$. If $x_i \ne y_i$ and $x_j = y_j$ for every $j \ne i$, then the grid cost of the pair $\{x, y\}$ with cost $w_j$ in coordinate $j$ is $w_i$.

results.title: Vertices of the Grassmann graph
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$, the vertices of the Grassmann graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$ are the $\ell$-dimensional linear subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$.

results.title: Grassmann graph over $\mathbb{F}_2$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$, the Grassmann graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$ has as vertices the $\ell$-dimensional linear subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, and two distinct such subspaces $L$ and $L'$ are adjacent when $\dim(L \cap L') = \ell - 1$.

results.title: Grassmann vertices between two subspaces
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $\ell$ and linear subspaces $A$ and $B$ of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)[A, B]$ is the finite set of vertices $L$ of the Grassmann graph $\mathrm{Gr}(k, \ell)$, that is of $\ell$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^k$, with $A \subseteq L \subseteq B$. If $A \not\subseteq B$ the set is empty.

results.title: Edge expansion of a vertex set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $S \subseteq V$ be nonempty. Let $d$ be the degree in $G$ of a fixed vertex of $S$, chosen once for each $S$. The expansion of $S$ is the rational number $\Phi_G(S) = |E(S, V \setminus S)| / (d \cdot |S|)$, where $E(S, V \setminus S)$ is the set of edges of $G$ with one endpoint in $S$ and the other in $V \setminus S$; it is $0$ when $d = 0$.

results.title: Labels of the reversal component
results.caption: Inductive

results.title: Program of the reversal component
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The multi-stack program over the stacks $X$ and $O$, both with alphabet $\mathrm{Bool}$, with a Boolean internal state: at label mv it moves the bits of $X$ one at a time onto $O$ (reversing them) and then goes to drop; at drop it pops $O$ once and goes to done; at done it halts.

results.title: The reversal component
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The component machine with two stacks, the input stack $X$ and the output stack $O$, both over the alphabet $\mathrm{Bool}$; the three labels mv, drop and done; the program that moves the bits of $X$ onto $O$ (reversing them), pops $O$ once and halts; and the stack list $[X, O]$.

results.title: Running the reversal component
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit list $x$, the program of the reversal component, started at label mv with internal state false, with the bits of $x$ on the input stack $X$ and every other stack empty, reaches label done within at most $|x| + 2$ steps, with some internal state and some stacks whose output stack $O$ holds the reversal of $x$ with its first entry removed.

part.title: Ambiguity of context-free grammars
api: Leftmost derivations from a word of terminals are empty

results.title: Leftmost derivation
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar, $u$ a sentential form of $g$, $w$ a word of terminals and $r_1, \dots, r_n$ a list of rules over the terminals and nonterminals of $g$. The list $r_1, \dots, r_n$ is a leftmost derivation of $w$ from $u$ in $g$ when every $r_i$ is a production of $g$, and, starting from $u$ and for $i = 1, \dots, n$ in turn, the leftmost nonterminal of the current sentential form is the left-hand…

results.title: Ambiguous grammar
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A context-free grammar $g$ is ambiguous if some word of terminals $w$ has two leftmost derivations from the start symbol of $g$ that use different lists of rules.

results.title: Leftmost derivations are derivations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a sentential form $u$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ to a word of terminals $w$, then $u$ derives $w$ in $g$ (by zero or more rewriting steps).

results.title: Words with a leftmost derivation lie in the language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a word of terminals $w$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ from the start symbol of $g$, then $w$ belongs to the language of $g$.

results.title: Leftmost derivations from a word of terminals are empty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $u$ a word of terminals. If $u$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ with list of rules $\rho$ to a word of terminals $w$, then $\rho$ is the empty list and $w = u$.

results.title: Canonical inherently ambiguous context-free language
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The language `{a ^ i b ^ j c ^ k | i = j or j = k}` over the alphabet `Fin 3` (`0, 1, 2` for `a, b, c`): the standard inherently ambiguous context-free language.

results.title: Inherently ambiguous language
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A language is inherently ambiguous when it is context-free and every grammar generating it is ambiguous.

results.title: Inherently ambiguous example as a union of two languages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The example language is the union of `a ^ n b ^ n c ^ *` and `a ^ * b ^ n c ^ n`.

results.title: The example language is context-free
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The example language is context-free.

part.title: Fisher's decomposition of genetic variance
api: Orthogonality of dominance deviations in the second allele

results.title: Mean genotypic value under Hardy–Weinberg proportions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The mean genotypic value `μ = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j G i j` under Hardy–Weinberg proportions.

results.title: Average effect of an allele
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The average effect of allele `i`, `α i = ∑ j p j G i j - μ`: the mean value of the genotypes carrying `i` (the other gene drawn from the population) minus the population mean. This is the average excess; under Hardy–Weinberg proportions it is Fisher's average effect, the coefficient of the least-squares additive fit (`domVar_le_sum_sq`).

results.title: Dominance deviation of a genotype
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The dominance deviation `δ i j = G i j - μ - α i - α j`.

results.title: Genetic variance under Hardy–Weinberg proportions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The genetic variance `V_G = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j (G i j - μ) ²`.

results.title: Additive genetic variance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The additive genetic variance `V_A = 2 ∑ i p i α i ²`, the variance of the breeding value `α i + α j`.

results.title: Dominance variance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The dominance variance `V_D = ∑ i ∑ j p i p j δ i j ²`.

results.title: Decomposition of the genotypic value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decomposition `G i j = μ + α i + α j + δ i j` (an identity by definition of `δ`).

results.title: Average effects have mean zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The average effects have mean zero: `∑ i p i α i = 0`.

results.title: Orthogonality of dominance deviations in the second allele
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Orthogonality of the dominance deviations: `∑ j p j δ i j = 0` for every `i`.

results.title: Orthogonality of dominance deviations in the first allele
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Orthogonality of the dominance deviations for a symmetric genotypic value: `∑ i p i δ i j = 0` for every `j`.

results.title: Least squares (Fisher 1918)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Among all fits `c + a i + a j` of the genotypic value by a function additive over the two genes, the additive fitted genotypic value `μ + α i + α j` minimizes the weighted squared error `∑ p i p j (G i j - c - a i - a j) ²`; its error is `V_D`.

results.title: Fisher's variance decomposition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `V_G = V_A + V_D`.

results.title: Parent–offspring covariance of genotypic values
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The covariance of the genotypic values of a parent and its offspring: the parent has genotype `(i, j)` (frequency `p i p j`) and transmits `cond b i j` (each with probability `1/2`), and the offspring's other gene `k` comes from an unrelated mate (frequency `p k`).

results.title: Half-sib covariance of genotypic values
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The covariance of the genotypic values of half sibs: the common parent has genotype `(i, j)` and transmits `cond b i j` to one offspring and, independently, `cond b' i j` to the other; the second genes `k`, `l` come from two unrelated mates.

results.title: Full-sib covariance of genotypic values
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The covariance of the genotypic values of full sibs: the sire `(i, j)` and the dam `(k, l)` are unrelated; the first offspring receives `cond b i j` and `cond e k l`, the second, independently, `cond b' i j` and `cond e' k l`.

results.title: Parent and offspring (Fisher 1918)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `Cov(P, O) = V_A / 2`.

results.title: Half sibs (Fisher 1918)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `Cov(HS) = V_A / 4`.

results.title: Full sibs (Fisher 1918)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `Cov(FS) = V_A / 2 + V_D / 4`.

results.title: Allele frequencies at a biallelic locus
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Allele frequencies at a biallelic locus: `A₁` (`true`) has frequency `q₁` and `A₂` (`false`) has frequency `1 - q₁`.

results.title: Genotypic values at a biallelic locus on Falconer's scale
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Genotypic values at a biallelic locus on Falconer's scale: `A₁A₁ ↦ a`, `A₁A₂ ↦ d`, `A₂A₂ ↦ -a` (the origin is the midpoint of the homozygotes).

results.title: Additive variance at a biallelic locus (Falconer & Mackay 1996, ch. 8)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With `p = q₁` and `q = 1 - q₁`, `V_A = 2pq (a + d (q - p)) ²`. An algebraic identity, valid for every real `q₁`; it is a variance for `0 ≤ q₁ ≤ 1`.

results.title: Dominance variance at a biallelic locus (Falconer & Mackay 1996, ch. 8)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `V_D = (2pqd) ²`, for every real `q₁`.
